title: [Vantage Point] Tubig Pilipinas’ backdoor listing move opens into another suspension
summary: A dormant coal shell refashions itself into a piped-water holding enterprise

items: Tubig Pilipinas Holdings Inc. (TPHI) has transformed from a dormant coal shell into a water holding company by acquiring 100% of Tubig Pilipinas Group Inc. (TPGI) through a share swap, leading to significant changes in its corporate structure.

The Philippine Stock Exchange suspended TPHI's trading due to a dilution of public float below the mandated threshold, creating urgency for the company to restore its public float within six months to avoid delisting.

The acquisition of TPGI at a valuation of P6.646 billion raises concerns for minority shareholders, as the high multiples on book equity and trailing revenue for an unprofitable asset necessitate a successful equity offering to bridge the gap between private arrangements and public market expectations.

Tubig Pilipinas Holdings Inc. (TPHI, listed as TUBIG) has completed one of the local bourse’s most literal corporate metamorphoses: a dormant coal shell has been refashioned into a piped-water holding enterprise.

TPHI and Tubig Pilipinas Group Inc. (TPGI) are distinct corporate entities. TPHI is the publicly listed parent company whose shares trade on the exchange, while TPGI is the unlisted operating arm that develops, manages, and operates the underlying water distribution utilities.
With TPHI acquiring 100% of TPGI through a share swap, the investing public now holds its economic interest in the water assets indirectly through the listed shell.

Yet for ordinary minority shareholders watching from the sidelines, the initial dividend of this transformation is neither a buoyant commercial pipeline nor an invigorated business. It is a stock certificate they are legally barred from trading.
The Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) lifted the company’s extended suspension on October 14 after classifying the transaction as a backdoor listing. The reprieve proved ephemeral.
Just five trading sessions later, the bourse slapped TUBIG with another trading freeze because the share swap diluted the public float from 28.31% to 10.64%, well below the mandated 20% threshold.
Under the exchange’s amended rules, the company has a strict six-month cure period. Failure to restore the float within that compressed window triggers automatic delisting.

That timetable creates an immediate strategic disconnect. In its disclosures, TUBIG indicated plans to execute a follow-on public offering within a year of completing the swap. The exchange’s trading suspension sends a sharp counter-signal: the market will not wait that long.

The asset transaction was massive relative to the legacy corporate chassis. To acquire full control of operating subsidiary TPGI — owned equally by Pure Water Corporation and Quadwater Corporation — TPHI issued 66.46 billion new common shares at a par value of P0.10 each.
That pegged the acquisition value at P6.646 billion. The transaction handed the vendors a dominant 62.43% equity slice, ballooning total outstanding shares from 40 billion to 106.46 billion.

The resulting registry consolidates control into a few hands. Following the swap, Pure Water and Quadwater emerged with matching 37.65% stakes. Affiliate Pure Energy Holdings Corp. preserved a 4.69% toehold, while Dutch investment vehicle CEF2 A09 B.V. took 9.36%.
Together, this controlling bloc locks up 89.35% of the company. The legacy public float, stranded at an unchanged 11.33 billion shares, was relegated to a residual 10.64% corner.

The underlying arithmetic shows the sheer scale of the balance-sheet surgery required to cure the deficit. If the controlling shareholders execute a secondary placement, they must unload roughly 9.97 billion shares to the public.

If management opts for a primary offering, TUBIG would need to issue approximately 12.46 billion fresh shares, as the enlarged capital base demands higher share volume to reach 20%. Even at par, a primary issuance implies raising P1.25 billion in fresh equity—an ambitious capital call whose clearing price will test market appetite.

Consequently, that equity offering is no administrative footnote. It represents the solitary bridge between an engineered private arrangement and an active public market. More critically, its clearing price will deliver the first authentic, arm’s-length market test of the P6.646-billion valuation ascribed to TPGI.

For now, minority investors are asked to rely on faith. Filings indicate that Isla Lipana & Co. prepared an independent fairness opinion and valuation report dated January 29 using income and market approaches.

Yet published disclosures omit the substantive quantitative machinery: there are no disclosed discount rates, cash-flow projections, terminal growth assumptions, peer matrices, or sensitivity ranges. The complete valuation report was visibly missing from the public bundle.

This opacity is difficult to reconcile with TPGI’s audited financial position. The water business recorded 2025 revenue of P270.77 million, an operating loss of P27.53 million, and a net loss of P31.34 million.

Total equity stood at P818.18 million against P1.93 billion in long-term loans. Current liabilities of P1.87 billion eclipsed current assets of P1.15 billion, leaving a working capital deficit of roughly P719 million.

To be clear, the business is not a hollow shell. TPGI generated P193.01 million in operating cash flow in 2025 while absorbing P750.78 million in capital outlays. It operates 12 water distribution facilities, manages five projects under development, and projects P1.93 billion in capital expenditures through 2031. It is an authentic, capital-intensive infrastructure play undergoing buildout.

Yet an acquisition price of P6.646 billion represents 8.1 times book equity and 24.5 times trailing revenue for an unprofitable asset. While long-gestation utility concessions can justify premiums on future cash flows, those multiples make the underlying math essential reading for public investors whose holdings were diluted.
